correctness.rationale: Complete \(a\)-by-\(b\) Boolean-matrix enumeration with \(a+b\le9\) and exact canonicalization yields \(730\) connected bipartite isomorphism types at nine points, agreeing with independently known graph counts. Global synchronized 1-WL refinement gives exactly \(728\) equivalence classes, with two size-two classes represented by masks (106268,111290) and (237369,241337). A separate Python program recomputes uniqueness, connectedness and all class totals. Independent hand-checkable equitable partitions verify the witnesses have the same stable colour counts, while four-cycle counts (2,0) and (6,4) prove nonisomorphism. The standard Immerman–Lander result converts colour-refinement equivalence into C2 equivalence.

originality.rationale: Full-text materials of both 2015 counting-logic/colour-refinement classification papers were compared with the exact statement. They cover the general logical equivalence and equitable-cell obstructions but do not state the sharp relative nine-vertex threshold or exact two-doubleton census for connected bipartite graphs. OEIS A005142 gives the previously known total of 730 unlabelled connected bipartite graphs, not the 728 counting-logic classes. Searches of broader and direct equivalent formulations did not locate an earlier result; the finding is qualified by an explicit priority risk.
residual_risks: An earlier unindexed small-graph colour-refinement census could already contain the exact two doubletons or threshold.
The general identification theorems may facilitate an alternate short deduction of the finite result, but no prior source explicitly carrying out the complete restricted census was found.

value.rationale: The threshold is the first possible failure of C2 separation inside the natural, widely studied connected bipartite graph class. The complete first ambiguity layer is classified rather than sampled, and the two structural obstructions demonstrate that C2 may miss four-cycle counts and even girth while preserving connectivity and bipartiteness. This is a precise small-order expressivity benchmark, not an arbitrary slice or a repetition of the known isomorphism-type count.
